entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.3">Psa 47:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:2-4) “<hi type="italic">Thereupon the fear of Elohim</hi>” - so closes the chronicler (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>) the narrative of the defeat of the confederates -  <hi type="italic">“came upon all kingdoms of the countries, when they heard that Jahve had fought against the enemies of Israel.”</hi> The psalmist, however, does not in consequence or this particular event call upon them to tremble with fear, but to rejoice; for fear is an involuntary, extorted inward emotion, but joy a perfectly voluntary one. The true and final victory of Jahve consists not in a submission that is brought about by war and bloodshed and in consternation that stupefies the mind, but in a change in the minds and hearts of the peoples, so that they render joyful worship unto Him. In order that He may thus become the God of all peoples, He has first of all become the God of Israel; and Israel longs that this the purpose of its election may be attained. Out of this longing springs the call in Psa 47:2. The peoples are to show the God of revelation their joy by their gestures and their words; for Jahve is absolutely exalted (עליון, here it is a predicate, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56">Psa 78:56</reference> it is an attribute), terrible, and the sphere of His dominion has Israel for its central point, not, however, for its limit, but it extends over the whole earth. Everything must do homage to Him in His own people, whether willingly or by constraint. According to the tenses employed, what is affirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4">Psa 47:4</reference> appears to be a principle derived from their recent experience, inasmuch as the contemporary fact is not expressed in an historical form, but generalized and idealised. But יבחר, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference></hi>, is against this, since the choosing (election) is an act done once for all and not a continued act; we are therefore driven to regard the futures, as in Num 23:7; Jdg 2:1, as a statement of historical facts. Concerning ידבּר, He bent, made to stoop, vid., Psa 18:48. There is now no necessity for altering יבחר into ירחב, and more especially since this is not suited to the fact which has given occasion to the Psalm. On the contrary, יבחר presupposes that in the event of the day God has shown Himself to be a faithful and powerful Lord [<hi type="italic">lit.</hi> feudal Lord] of the land of Israel; the hostile confederation had thought of nothing less than driving Israel entirely out of its inheritance (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.11">2Ch 20:11</reference>). The Holy Land is called the pride (גּאון) of Jacob, as being the gift of grace of which this, the people of God’s love, can boast. In <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference> גאון יעקב has a different meaning (of the sin of pride), and again another sense in <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference> (of the glory of all Israel in accordance with the promise); here it is similar to Isa 13:19. את has a conjunctive accent instead of being followed by <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.12">Pro 3:12</reference> (these are the only three instances). The strophe which follows supports the view that the poet, in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.5">Psa 47:5</reference>, has a recent act of God before his mind.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.4-Ps.47.8">Psa 47:4-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:5-9) The ascent of God presupposes a previous descent, whether it be a manifestation of Himself in order to utter some promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.22">Gen 17:22</reference>; Jdg 13:20) or a triumphant execution of judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.19">Psa 68:19</reference>). So here: God has come down to fight on behalf of His people. They return to the Holy City and He to His throne, which is above on Zion, and higher still, is above in heaven. On בּתרוּעה and קול שׁופר cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.98.6">Psa 98:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.28">1Ch 15:28</reference>, but more especially <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Amo 2:2</reference>; for the “shout” is here the people’s shout of victory, and “the sound of the horn” the clear sound of the horns announcing the victory, with reference to the celebration of the victory in the Valley of praise and the homeward march amidst the clanging music (2Ch 20:26.). The poet, who has this festival of victory before his mind as having recently taken place, desires that the festive sounds may find an unending and boundless echo unto the glory of God. זמּר is first construed with the accusative as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.33">Psa 68:33</reference>, then with the dative. Concerning משׂכּיל = ᾠδὴ πενυματική (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Eph 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>), vid., on Psa 32:1. That which excites to songs of praise is Jahve’s dominion of the world which has just been made manifest. מלך is to be taken in just the same historical sense as ἐβασίλευσας, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Rev 11:15</reference>-18. What has taken place is a prelude of the final and visible entering upon the kingdom, the announcement of which the New Testament seer there hears. God has come down to earth, and after having obtained for Himself a recognition of His dominion by the destruction of the enemies of Israel, He has ascended again in visible kingly glory. <hi type="italic">Imago conscensi a Messia throni gloriae</hi>, says Chr. Aug. Crusius, <hi type="italic">tune erat deportatio arcae faederis in sedem regni</hi>.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.47.9">Psa 47:9</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_47:10) In the mirror of the present event, the poet reads the great fact of the conversion of all peoples to Jahve which closes the history of the world. The nobles of the peoples (נדיבי with the twofold meaning of <hi type="italic">generosi</hi>), the “shields (i.e., the lords who are the defenders of their people) of the earth” (Hos 4:18), enter into the society of the people of the God of Abraham; πέρας αἱ πρὸς τὸν πατριάρχην Ἀβραὰμ ἔλαβον ὑποσχέσεις, as Theodoret observes. The promise concerning the blessing of the tribes of the nations in the seed of the patriarch is being fulfilled; for the nobles draw the peoples who are protected by them after themselves. It is unnecessary to read עם instead of עם with Ewald, and following the lxx and Syriac; and it is also inadmissible, since one does not say נאסף עם, but ל or אל. Even Eusebius has rightly praised Symmachus and Theodotion, because they have translated the ambiguous ἀμ by λαὸς (τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἀβραάμ), viz., as being a nominative of the effect or result, as it is also understood by the Targum, Jerome, Luther, and most of the Jewish expositors, and among modern expositors by Crusius, Hupfeld, and Hitzig: They gather and band themselves together as a people or into a people of the God of Abraham, they submit themselves with Israel to the one God who is proved to be so glorious.<note placement="foot">It is also accented accordingly, viz., נאספו with <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi>, which (and in this respect it is distinguished from <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>) makes a pause; and this is then followed by the supplementing clause with <hi type="italic">Zinnor, Galgal</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Olewejored</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen9494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> The conclusion (v. 11) reminds one of the song of Hannah, 1Sa 2:8. Thus universal homage is rendered to Him: He is gone up in triumph, and is in consequence thereof highly exalted (נעלה, <hi type="italic">3rd</hi> <hi type="italic">praet</hi>., the result of consequence of the עלה in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.6">Psa 47:6</reference>). The inaccessibleness of the City of God <div eID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14">Psa 48:1-14</reference> is also a song of thanksgiving for victory. It is connected with <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9">Psa 47:1-9</reference> by the fundamental thought of the exaltation of Jahve above the peoples of the earth; but is distinguished from them both in this respect, viz., that, in accordance with the favourite characteristic of Korahitic poetry, the song of thanksgiving for victory has become a song in praise of Jerusalem, the glorious and strong city, protected by God who sits enthroned in it. The historical occasion is the same. The mention of the kings points to an army of confederates; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.10">Psa 48:10</reference> points to the gathering held in the temple before the setting out of the army; and the figurative representation of the hostile powers by the shattered ships of Tarshish does not apply to any period so well as to the time of Jehoshaphat. The points of coincidence between this Psalm (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.8">Psa 48:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.13">Psa 48:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.18">Isa 33:18</reference>; v. 15 with <reference osisRef="Isa.33.22">Isa 33:22</reference>), as well as <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference>, and Isaiah do not prove that he is its author.  <chapter eID="Ps.47"/> <div eID="gen9496" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: Psa 47:9 (Hebrew_Bible_47:10) In the mirror of the present event, the poet reads the great fact of the conversion of all peoples to Jahve which closes the history of the world. The nobles of the peoples (נדיבי with the twofold meaning of generosi ), the “shields (i.e., the lords who are the defenders of their people) of the earth” (Hos 4:18), enter into the society of the people of the God of Abraham; πέρας αἱ πρὸς τὸν πατριάρχην Ἀβραὰμ ἔλαβον ὑποσχέσεις, as Theodoret observes. The promise concerning the blessing of the tribes of the nations in the seed of the patriarch is being fulfilled; for the nobles draw the peoples who are protected by them after themselves. It is unnecessary to read עם instead of עם with Ewald, and following the lxx and Syriac; and it is also inadmissible, since one does not say נאסף עם, but ל or אל. Even Eusebius has rightly praised Symmachus and Theodotion, because they have translated the ambiguous ἀμ by λαὸς (τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἀβραάμ), viz., as being a nominative of the effect or result, as it is also understood by the Targum, Jerome, Luther, and most of the Jewish expositors, and among modern expositors by Crusius, Hupfeld, and Hitzig: They gather and band themselves together as a people or into a people of the God of Abraham, they submit themselves with Israel to the one God who is proved to be so glorious. It is also accented accordingly, viz., נאספו with Rebia magnum , which (and in this respect it is distinguished from Mugrash ) makes a pause; and this is then followed by the supplementing clause with Zinnor, Galgal , and Olewejored . The conclusion (v. 11) reminds one of the song of Hannah, 1Sa 2:8. Thus universal homage is rendered to Him: He is gone up in triumph, and is in consequence thereof highly exalted (נעלה, 3rd praet ., the result of consequence of the עלה in Psa 47:6 ). The inaccessibleness of the City of God Psa 48:1-14 is also a song of thanksgiving for victory. It is connected with Psa 46:1-11 and Psa 47:1-9 by the fundamental thought of the exaltation of Jahve above the peoples of the earth; but is distinguished from them both in this respect, viz., that, in accordance with the favourite characteristic of Korahitic poetry, the song of thanksgiving for victory has become a song in praise of Jerusalem, the glorious and strong city, protected by God who sits enthroned in it. The historical occasion is the same. The mention of the kings points to an army of confederates; Psa 48:10 points to the gathering held in the temple before the setting out of the army; and the figurative representation of the hostile powers by the shattered ships of Tarshish does not apply to any period so well as to the time of Jehoshaphat. The points of coincidence between this Psalm (cf. Psa 48:7 with Isa 33:14 ; Psa 48:8 with Isa 33:21 ; Psa 48:13 with Isa 33:18 ; v. 15 with Isa 33:22 ), as well as Psa 46:1-11 , and Isaiah do not prove that he is its author.
